h: Gilt, Glamour and a Little Bit of Shakespeare
p: The Ballroom opened with the Tower in 1894, and the lavish interior you see today owes a lot to Frank Matcham, the celebrated theatre architect who redesigned it at the end of the 1890s. Look up and you'll see painted ceilings, gilded balconies and sparkling chandeliers, and above the stage there's a line from Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis: 'Bid me discourse, I will enchant thine ear.' It's the perfect motto for a room built around music.

That music has its own legend too. Reginald Dixon, the organist nicknamed 'Mr Blackpool', played the Tower Wurlitzer for decades from the 1930s, and his signature tune 'I Do Like to Be Beside the Seaside' became one of the most famous sounds of the British seaside. The organ rising from beneath the stage is still a moment that raises goosebumps.

Even if you're not a dancer, it's worth sitting at a table for a while and watching the regulars. Some of them glide around like they've been doing it all their lives, because they probably have. Comfy shoes are wise if you plan to join in, and a camera is a must for those balcony shots.

Out the doors, the Promenade, piers and trams are waiting, and the Winter Gardens, another grand Victorian entertainment venue, is only a short walk inland if you can't get enough of the old-school glamour.
